query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles form successfully when a support that generates spillover hydrogen enables the rapid, synchronous reduction of metal precursors. This simultaneous reduction minimizes differences in reduction kinetics between noble and base metals, thereby suppressing phase separation or intermetallic formation and promoting homogeneous alloying.
generation.material_initial_state: A multimetal precursor mixture (including noble metal salts along with base metal salts) dispersed on a support; for comparison, the same precursor mixture is deposited on a support lacking spillover activity.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatment at a temperature low enough to promote spillover-induced hydrogen generation (and thus fast, synchronized reduction) on the reducible oxide support, while keeping the same conditions on an inert support.
generation.conditions: The approach applies when the precursor mixture contains metals with mismatched reduction potentials and when the support is capable of producing spillover hydrogen at moderate temperatures. The initial metal composition and processing conditions (aside from the support’s spillover ability) remain unchanged.
generation.structural_mediator: The rapid formation and migration of spillover hydrogen species on the reducible oxide support mediates simultaneous nucleation of all metals, ensuring that the atomic mixing occurs before significant diffusion-driven segregation can set in.
generation.mechanism: The oxide support’s spillover effect synchronizes the reduction of disparate metal ions by providing high reduction potentials via hydrogen spillover. This mechanism achieves simultaneous nucleation, enabling the formation of a single-phase, homogeneous alloy nanoparticle rather than distinct phases or intermetallic compounds.
generation.predicted_outcome: When using a spillover-capable support, the resultant HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a homogeneous solid solution with well-controlled size and distribution, whereas on an inert support the reduction will occur sequentially, leading to phase separation or the formation of intermetallic compounds.
generation.baseline: Under identical thermal treatment, precursor mixtures on an inert support (without spillover activity) will show less homogeneous alloying, with signs of phase segregation or multiple phases in XRD and compositional analysis.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles synthesized under conditions where reduction kinetics are inherently mismatched and when the support can actively mediate hydrogen spillover. It may not apply to systems where all metal precursors reduce at nearly the same rate or where high-temperature annealing (without spillover influence) is the dominant synthesis route.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature window and efficiency of spillover required for successful synchronization may vary with different metal combinations and support characteristics, which necessitates further parameterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled comparison by synthesizing HEA nanoparticles from the same metal precursor mixture under identical thermal treatment conditions on (a) a spillover-active support (e.g., TiO2) and (b) an inert support (e.g., SiO2).
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy combined with energy dispersive spectroscopy for assessing nanoparticle morphology and compositional homogeneity
In situ spectroscopic monitoring (e.g., XANES) to track reduction kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles synthesized on the spillover-active support do not show significantly improved phase homogeneity (i.e., a single solid solution phase) compared to those from the inert support, or if both systems display equivalent phase separation behaviors, then the hypothesis that spillover-induced synchronized reduction governs successful HEA nanoparticle formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Our own group has previously demonstrated that TiO2 is a promising platform for the synthesis of non-equilibrium binary alloy NPs, such as RuNi and RhCu, which are essentially immiscible at equilibrium due to the positive enthalpies of formation of their solid solution alloys,. However, the highly specific formation of binary alloy NPs based on combinations of normally immiscible noble and base metals can be achieved with the assistance of the strong spillover effect obtained from TiO2. Using this oxide allows spillover hydrogen species with high reduction potentials to be generated from noble metals (Ru or Rh) and to rapidly migrate to and reduce base metals (Ni or Cu) at low temperatures. In the present work, we developed and demonstrated that this facile strategy can be applied to the synthesis of TiO2-supported HEA NPs. Specifically, CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs on TiO2 displayed high activity and outstanding stability during the CO2 hydrogenation reaction. This study also elucidated the specific mechanism responsible for the formation of HEA NPs, based on in situ characterization techniques.
